facts.claim: The Muse was released October 1, 2013 as The Wood Brothers' fifth studio album. It was produced by Buddy Miller, with Zac Brown as executive producer, and recorded and mixed by Mike Poole.
The album was recorded at Southern Ground Studios in Nashville. The 2013 original came out on Zac Brown's Southern Ground label. The 2LP vinyl reissue is listed on Indirecto.

Chris Wood played vocals, bass, harmonica, guitar and mandolin. Oliver Wood played vocals, guitar and mandocello. Jano Rix played vocals, drums, shuitar, percussion, melodica and piano. Guests were Buddy Miller (baritone guitar), Regina and Anne McCrary (background vocals), Jim Hoke (sax), Bill Huber (trombone) and Steve Herrman (trumpet).

The label's press release says the title track is Oliver Wood's most tender and autobiographical songwriting to date. He sings of his newborn child as his "finest work yet", over bowed bass and melodica.

In track-by-track notes, the band describes the title track as very personal but universal. They say it had to be spare, with no drums and no beat, so the music could follow the fluidity of the words.

Oliver Wood told Billboard that the song began as a piece of music, with its melody and structure written first. He said a muse can be positive or very dark, and the song is about the positives and negatives that inspire artists. He declined to give specifics about the inspiration.
The album was recorded the old-fashioned way, with the trio circled around a tree of microphones. Even the lead vocals were recorded on the spot.

Chris Wood called The Muse the first album recorded with drummer/multi-instrumentalist Jano Rix, and said it was the birth of the Wood Brothers as a trio. Oliver Wood said it was their first studio album with their own full-time drummer.
Oliver Wood called Buddy Miller a pleasure to work with and described him as quiet but wise and Yoda-like.

The Muse gave the band its first Billboard chart success, reaching the folk, country, indie and rock charts in late 2013. The band was by then Nashville-based, with Oliver having moved in 2012 and Chris following.

Oliver and Chris Wood grew up in Boulder, Colorado. Their father was a molecular and developmental biologist who also performed folk music, and their mother wrote poetry. Chris is also known from Medeski, Martin & Wood.

research.lineage: The Wood Brothers sit in the American roots, folk and blues tradition, with a Band-style, New Orleans/Memphis/Muscle Shoals flavour. Reviewers compare the horn-laden tracks to The Band, and the group's roots are in blues, jazz and gospel.

draft:
Three rooms, three times the same seat. **The Muse** opens with a narrator perched on "this never-made bed," moves him to the end of a dirty old bar, and finally sets him down in a hospital room. Each verse ends with the same hedged prayer, "Thank God, whoever you are," a thank-you sent to no fixed address. That phrase carries the whole song. The gratitude is real, but it comes out sideways. It's tucked inside a conditional (*if I was thinking, I'd be thinking*), and the refrain explains why: thinking is the last thing you want to do. Some moments are too good to look at directly. Others are too bad.

The middle verse is where the song earns its sweetness. The muse who stood in the doorway brushing her hair is now "all alone on the other side of town," and what he thanks God for is the whiskey. The refrain turns from sweet to sad but keeps calling it true, and he doesn't apologize or explain. Oliver Wood told Billboard that a muse can be positive or very dark, and he declined to say what happened. The song doesn't say either. It just lets the bar sit between the bedroom and the delivery room, so the joy at the end feels like something that was in doubt.

Then the third verse lands. He's "shedding a tear for the bride and groom," grieving the couple they were even as the baby starts to cry. And then: "It's my finest work yet, if today I should die." It's a songwriter's boast and a new parent's terror in one breath, pride and mortality holding hands. The label called it Oliver Wood's most tender and autobiographical writing yet, and you can hear him reach for a craftsman's word, *work*, because the plain feeling is too big.

The band said the song had to be spare, with no drums and no beat, so the music could follow the words. That's what you get. A fingerpicked acoustic pattern rolls in slow arpeggios over a steady bass, the groove sways rather than pushes, and the arrangement around it adds bowed bass and melodica. Wood's voice is clear with a little rasp at the edges, relaxed enough to sound like he's singing it to the room. And he was. Buddy Miller produced the album at Southern Ground in Nashville, with the trio circled around a tree of microphones and lead vocals cut on the spot. The warm, close room tone is that circle. It's American roots music with the horns and the Band-style strut stripped away, folk at its plainest.

It sticks because it gives you permission to feel grateful without understanding, to thank whoever's listening for the good years and the bad nights alike.
